title: Understanding Pedestrian Fatal-Crash Outcomes: Temporal Patterns, Vehicle Characteristics, and Contributing Factors in New York City (2021–2025)
content: Background: Pedestrian fatalities remain a critical urban transportation safety concern, with crash outcomes potentially influenced by temporal conditions, vehicle characteristics, and contributing factors. This study investigates the associations between these characteristics and pedestrian fatal-crash outcomes in New York City (NYC) from 2021 to 2025, with particular attention to nighttime occurrence and solar darkness.Methods: Police-reported collision data from NYC Open Data were analyzed. Of 486,548 collision records, 42,911 pedestrian casualty crashes were identified, including 606 crashes involving at least one pedestrian fatality. Geographic information system (GIS) techniques were used to recover missing borough information. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression models were employed to examine temporal patterns, first-recorded vehicle types, and police-reported contributing factors. Solar darkness was classified using crash-specific sunrise and sunset times for 40,578 crashes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated across five regression specifications.Results: The fatal-crash proportion was higher during nighttime (2.62%) than daytime (1.03%). In the primary regression model, nighttime was associated with increased odds of pedestrian fatal-crash occurrence (aOR = 2.55, 95% CI: 2.16–3.00), and the association persisted after additional adjustment for vehicle types and police-reported contributing factors (aOR = 2.72, 95% CI: 2.30–3.23). Exploratory analyses identified elevated fatal-crash odds for crashes involving first-recorded heavy/commercial vehicles, buses, pickup trucks, and SUVs/station wagons. Solar darkness was also associated with higher fatal-crash odds (aOR = 2.59, 95% CI: 2.16–3.09), and the association remained significant after adjustment for calendar month and five time-of-day categories (aOR = 2.32, 95% CI: 1.67–3.22). Weekend associations were less consistent across model specifications.Conclusions: Nighttime was consistently associated with increased odds of fatal outcomes among reported pedestrian casualty crashes, while vehicle characteristics and police-reported contributing factors revealed additional differences in crash outcomes. Solar darkness provided complementary information beyond conventional clock-based nighttime definitions. These findings support integrating temporal, vehicle-related, and environmental characteristics into urban pedestrian safety assessments to better identify conditions associated with fatal crashes.
